title: GPA-VGGT:Adapting VGGT to Large scale Localization by self-Supervised learning with Geometry and Physics Aware loss
authors: Yangfan Xu,Lilian Zhang,Xiaofeng He,Pengdong Wu,Wenqi Wu,Jun Mao
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Transformer-based general visual geometry frameworks have shown promising performance in camera pose estimation and 3D scene understanding.
Recent advancements in Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) models have shown great promise in camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. However, these models typically rely on ground truth labels for training, posing challenges when adapting to unlabeled and unseen scenes. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised framework to train VGGT with unlabeled data, thereby enhancing its localization capability in large-scale environments. To achieve this, we extend conventional pair-wise relations to sequence-wise geometric constraints for self-supervised learning. Specifically, in each sequence, we sample multiple source frames and geometrically project them onto different target frames, which improves temporal feature consistency. We formulate physical photometric consistency and geometric constraints as a joint optimization loss to circumvent the requirement for hard labels. By training the model with this proposed method, not only the local and global cross-view attention layers but also the camera and depth heads can effectively capture the underlying multi-view geometry. Experiments demonstrate that the model converges within hundreds of iterations and achieves significant improvements in large-scale localization.
Our code will be released at https://github.com/X-yangfan/GPA-VGGT.
introduction:
Estimating camera pose and scene geometry is a central problem in computer vision and underlies a wide range of applications, including visual localization, autonomous driving, and large-scale 3D scene understanding. Classical geometric pipelines, such as Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and SLAM, achieve strong performance through explicit geometric modeling and optimization [1], but often rely on carefully designed components and struggle to scale robustly in complex real-world environments. Learning-based approaches aim to overcome these limitations by enabling end-to-end training and improved generalization; however, learning physically consistent geometry at scale remains a challenging open problem.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, existing learning-based methods for pose and depth estimation can be broadly categorized into two groups.
The first category comprises conventional self-supervised approaches that learn depth and camera motion from temporally adjacent image pairs via photometric reconstruction [2, 3] (Fig. 1a).
While appealing for their label-free training, these methods suffer from inherent limitations in both supervision scope and architectural capacity.
On the one hand, relying primarily on pair-wise or short-range constraints prevents these models from enforcing geometric consistency across longer temporal spans, as they effectively treat each time step in isolation.
On the other hand, the majority of these frameworks employ Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) as backbones.
Constrained by their local receptive fields and lack of long-range dependency modeling, CNNs struggle to effectively capture global context or encode information from extended sequences.
Consequently, accumulated trajectory drift and scale inconsistency commonly emerge when such methods are applied to large-scale environments [4].

The second category comprises recent Transformer-based geometry frameworks, exemplified by VGGT [5] and its extension to full system pipelines like VGGT-SLAM [6].
Unlike the CNN-based approaches mentioned above, these models leverage global attention mechanisms, theoretically resolving the issue of limited receptive fields and offering the capacity to capture long-range geometric dependencies.
However, unlocking this potential in self-supervised settings remains a significant challenge.
Current Transformer-based methods, including VGGT and VGGT-SLAM, predominantly rely on large-scale ground-truth labels to establish geometric priors.
When applied to unlabeled video sequences without such supervision, their optimization becomes unstable; the high-capacity attention layers, lacking explicit structural guidance, tend to overfit to local photometric cues rather than learning consistent global geometry.
Similar limitations persist in point-map regression models like DUSt3R [7], which, despite their powerful pairwise matching capabilities, lack the explicit temporal constraints necessary for enforcing trajectory coherence over extended sequences.
Consequently, a critical gap remains: while the architecture has evolved to support global reasoning, the self-supervised training paradigms are still constrained by local, pairwise supervision, failing to fully exploit the temporal context available in large-scale video data.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel self-supervised learning strategy that elevates supervision from local frame pairs to structured 3D spatial consistency across sequences.
Crucially, we incorporate a robust physical screening mechanism to explicitly handle the noise inherent in large-scale environments, such as dynamic objects, occlusions, and sudden illumination variations.
This loss-driven formulation aligns the optimization objective with the underlying physical structure of the scene, allowing the model to selectively learn from reliable geometric cues while automatically discarding misleading signals.
As a result, the model learns more stable and scalable geometric representations, leading to improved performance and generalization in large-scale environments.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a novel self-supervised framework designed to adapt the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer (VGGT) for large-scale localization using purely unlabeled data. This effectively bridges the gap between data-hungry Transformer architectures and the deployment in unseen, wild environments without ground-truth labels.

We propose a multi-sequence geometric consistency strategy reinforced by a physics-based hard selection mechanism. By dynamically filtering out unreliable supervision from occluded or dynamic regions and enforcing cross-window scale alignment, we effectively mitigate the trajectory drift and environmental noise issues inherent in long-sequence self-supervised learning.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed training strategy enables the model to converge efficiently within hundreds of iterations. The adapted model exhibits significant improvements in localization accuracy and strong generalization capabilities across large-scale datasets.

Self-supervised learning of depth and camera motion has been extensively studied as a way to avoid reliance on ground-truth geometric annotations. Early works exploit photometric reconstruction between temporally adjacent frames to jointly learn monocular depth and ego-motion [2]. Subsequent methods improve robustness by incorporating additional geometric constraints, such as 3D point cloud consistency [4] or refined view synthesis objectives [3]. Despite their success, these approaches typically operate on short frame pairs or limited temporal windows, enforcing only local geometric consistency. As a result, they often suffer from accumulated drift, scale inconsistency, and degraded performance when applied to large-scale scenes or long sequences.

Several works attempt to extend self-supervised learning beyond two-frame settings by introducing temporal aggregation or recurrent modeling. However, most methods still rely on pairwise supervision and lack explicit mechanisms to enforce global geometric consistency across multiple sequences, which remains a key limitation in large-scale self-supervised geometry learning.

In parallel, learning-based camera pose estimation has been explored through direct pose regression. PoseNet and its variants demonstrate that camera poses can be regressed directly from single images using convolutional neural networks [8, 9]. While these methods offer simple and efficient pipelines, later analyses reveal fundamental limitations in accuracy and generalization due to the absence of explicit geometric reasoning [10]. These findings suggest that geometric structure cannot be reliably learned through direct supervision on poses alone, motivating approaches that incorporate stronger geometric constraints.

Recent advances in transformer architectures have enabled more expressive modeling of visual geometry. VGGT proposes a unified transformer-based framework for learning depth and pose within a general-purpose geometry representation [5]. Building upon this idea, VGGSfM integrates classical structure-from-motion principles into a learned pipeline, bridging traditional multi-view geometry and deep learning [11]. These approaches demonstrate the potential of transformer-based models for geometric reasoning, yet extending them to large-scale scenes remains challenging due to optimization difficulty and the lack of strong cross-sequence geometric supervision.

In parallel, fully learned geometry systems such as DUSt3R show that dense 3D correspondences and geometry can be inferred from image pairs in a data-driven manner [7]. While effective for local and pairwise geometry estimation, these methods typically focus on limited view configurations and do not directly address globally consistent pose and depth prediction across long sequences.

In contrast to prior work, our approach induces geometric reasoning in a general-purpose transformer framework through structured, multi-sequence 3D self-supervised loss design. By enforcing cross-temporal and multi-view physical consistency without introducing additional architectural components, our method enables scalable and stable geometry learning in large-scale environments.

This effectively bridges the gap between data-hungry Transformer architectures and the deployment in unseen, wild environments without ground-truth labels.

2. We propose a multi-sequence geometric consistency strategy reinforced by a physics-based hard selection mechanism. By dynamically filtering out unreliable supervision from occluded or dynamic regions and enforcing cross-window scale alignment, we effectively mitigate the trajectory drift and environmental noise issues inherent in long-sequence self-supervised learning.

1. 现有的自监督学习方法在大规模场景中难以有效捕捉全局几何一致性。  
2. 传统几何方法依赖于精确的标签，限制了在未标记场景中的适应能力。  
3. 需要一种新的方法来提高自监督学习在大规模环境中的稳定性和准确性。  

【前人的工作如何解决该问题，存在哪些空白】  
1. 早期的自监督方法依赖于临近帧的光度重建，但仅限于局部几何一致性。  
2. 现有的Transformer基础模型如VGGT，虽然具有全局注意力机制，但仍依赖于大量的地面真相标签，导致在无标签序列中的优化不稳定。  

【提出了什么创新的方法】  
我们提出了一种新颖的自监督学习框架，通过引入多序列几何一致性策略和物理一致性损失，提升了VGGT在大规模定位中的能力。具体而言，我们通过对多个源帧进行几何投影，增强了时间特征的一致性，并采用物理光度一致性和几何约束的联合优化损失，避免了对硬标签的需求。实验结果表明，该模型在几百次迭代内收敛，并在大规模定位中显著提高了准确性和泛化能力。

title: An Efficient Insect-inspired Approach for Visual Point-goal Navigation
abstract: In this work we develop a novel insect-inspired agent for visual point-goal navigation. This combines abstracted models of two insect brain structures that have been implicated, respectively, in associative learning and path integration. We draw an analogy between the formal benchmark of the Habitat point-goal navigation task and the ability of insects to learn and refine visually guided paths around obstacles between a discovered food location and their nest. We demonstrate that the simple insect-inspired agent exhibits performance comparable to recent SOTA models at many orders of magnitude less computational cost. Testing in a more realistic simulated environment shows the approach is robust to perturbations.
introduction:
Goal-directed navigation requires an intelligent agent, artificial or biological,
to reach a goal through motion planning and control.
It has wide real-world applications in mobile robots,
from indoor to outdoor, spanning ground, underground, marine, and aerial scenarios.
One of its particular forms, point-goal navigation, has recently been standardised and popularised by the annual Habitat navigation challenges
‘to benchmark and accelerate progress in embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI)’ Savva et al. (2019).
At the start of point-goal navigation, the agent is provided with the explicit position (two-dimensional coordinates) of the goal (a point with a small catchment area)
and tasked to reach it without an a priori map.
In an obstacle-free environment, point-goal navigation can be solved by Path Integration (PI), i.e., dead reckoning, solely.
In a more complex environment, however,
the agent must employ other techniques to perceive obstacles (or traversable space) and take appropriate, ideally predictive, actions to find and follow an efficient path towards the goal.
Typically, the Habitat point-goal navigation task considers an agent relying primarily on vision from a front-facing camera mounted on a robot.

Two contrasting solutions have been widely adopted over the years.
A traditional approach is to create, update, and utilise a map on the fly,
i.e., perform visual Simultaneous Localisation And Mapping (SLAM).
As the map grows in size and fidelity, motion planning becomes less error-prone.
More recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches have increased in popularity,
often making the assumption that there is no need for an explicit map.
In particular, an End-to-end RL agent is expected to learn the direct correspondence between sensory inputs and (desired) control outputs,
using general-purpose RL methods.
Notably, the State-Of-The-Art (SOTA) agent,
reported to achieve perfect performance in the Habitat point-goal navigation task Ramakrishnan et al. (2021),
was obtained by RL.
More specifically, Wijmans et al. (2019) developed a near-perfect agent by massively scaling up Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO), the de facto standard method of deep RL, into Decentralised Distributed PPO (DDPPO), and later Ramakrishnan et al. (2021) obtained the perfect agent with the same DDPPO method but using a larger and more accurately curated dataset of virtual scenes.

Here we adopt a third approach by considering a direct parallel to point-goal navigation observed in the behaviour of insects, such as ants, attempting to return to their nest after foraging.
Many insects are able to maintain, through PI, an estimate of their position relative to the nest over long journeys away from it, and will attempt to return on a straight line towards it when food is located Müller and Wehner (1988).
Moreover, during this return, the insect acquires visual information Collett et al. (1992) that improves its efficiency in negotiating obstacles Wystrach et al. (2011), leading to faster returns along improved paths on subsequent trips Freas and Cheng (2025).
Recent neuroethological and modelling studies have established plausible accounts of the neural circuits supporting these capabilities in insects,
with a focus on two brain structures that are conserved and anatomically stereotypical across insect species.
In particular, the Mushroom Body (MB) is specialised in associative learning Aso et al. (2014a); Webb (2024) and novelty (familiarity) detection (Hattori et al., 2017),
and the Central compleX (CX) in PI and motion planning Stone et al. (2017) (see Webb (2019) for a recent review).

Over the last decade, the CX has been clearly established as the ‘compass’ circuit in the insect brain, combining multi-modal sensory inputs and self motion to maintain an estimate of heading direction with respect to an external reference frame and to control steering towards an internally specified goal direction Hulse et al. (2021). A minimal augmentation of this circuit provides a basis by which an insect could integrate its velocity over a foraging journey Stone et al. (2017), i.e., perform PI to estimate its own location and use this to move towards any location specified in the same reference coordinates Le Moël et al. (2019). Models of this circuit have shown its efficacy for such point-goal navigation
Goldschmidt et al. (2017); Sun et al. (2020); Goulard et al. (2023); Wystrach (2023),
including real-world tests on a aerial robot Stankiewicz and Webb (2020). However, this work has either neglected obstacles or added simple obstacle avoidance mechanisms to negogiate obstacles that prevent direct movement towards the goal Baddeley et al. (2012); Sun et al. (2023).

The insect’s ability to memorise and follow visually familiar routes has been independently explained as deploying a ‘visual compass’, which operates in a fundamentally different way. As first proposed by (Philippides et al., 2011; Baddeley et al., 2012), this involves memorisation of multiple panoramic views and the use of template matching Labrosse (2006)
to estimate view familiarity/novelty and thus align to the route direction.
Ardin et al. (2016) explicitly identified a neural circuit known as the MB as a plausible substrate for this memory in the insect brain.
In addition to follow-up works on route following Kodzhabashev and Mangan (2015); Steinbeck et al. (2024); Lu et al. (2025), the same idea of the MB being a learnable visual compass is also applied to or corroborated by works on visual homing,
similar to point-goal navigation but the agent can rely only on vision (no odometry) in testing and the same scene is used in training and in testing Möller (2000).

In some of these MB models, route following has been combined with (non-visual) obstacle avoidance to improve robustness.
An agent can be first guided along a route once and thus implicitly learns a route that avoids obstacles (the ‘teach and repeat’ task in robot navigation) Lu et al. (2025).
Or, an agent can perform visual route learning during its initial homing attempt that does not rely on vision, but guided by PI and obstacle avoidance (Baddeley et al., 2012).
Although this implementation combines the functions of CX and MB,
there is a hard switch from the first traversal (using CX for homing and MB for visual learning) to subsequent traversals (using MB only for visual route following).
Recently, several existing models explore more organic integration of CX and MB circuits, demonstrating emergent behaviours of such agents, e.g., automatic switch from PI to visual homing when displaced to an arbitrary position, maintaining goal approaching locomotion when target object is temporarily obscured or removed Sun et al. (2020); Goulard et al. (2023).
However, all these models have an initial training phase and,
consequently, do not address how a ‘correct’ route is formed in the first place.
This question was more thoroughly studied in Freas and Cheng (2017); Freas and Spetch (2019); Clement et al. (2024); Freas and Cheng (2025).
In particular, Clement et al. (2024) explicitly demonstrated ‘ants learn continuously the routes … in one trial’ by behavioural experiments
and emulated the continuous learning and navigating of ants with the first-ever computational (non-neural) model with no prior training.

Here, we aim to develop an integrated model of these two insect navigation circuits (CX and MB) and assess the performance in realistic indoor robotic point-goal navigation simulations.
In brief, the CX is responsible for determining control signals based on desired (goal-directed) and actual orientations,
while the MB learns the association between visual inputs and collisions
and uses the learnt association to modulate the CX computation.
We hypothesise that, starting with zero prior memory,
our model can gradually learn to avoid obstacles in a predictive manner,
improving its route towards a goal even on the first trial, but increasingly so after repetition,
which may even lead to a successful trial after failures.
We first test our model in the Habitat simulator Savva et al. (2019) (offering the standardised point-goal navigation task of the 2019 Habitat Challenge),
permitting direct performance comparison between our model and others reported in recent literature.
We then deploy our model in the iGibson simulator Li et al. (2022), which offers a more realistic physics engine than Habitat,
to examine the contributions from the model components through ablation studies
and the model’s robustness in steering by adding artificial noise and bias.

This paper is organised as follows:
§2.1 introduces our insect-inspired model,
§2.2 describes the experimental setup,
§3 presents the main experiment results,
and §4 discusses the implications.
